title: EDA’s Future Is Evidence-Driven Automation
gist: AI's biggest EDA opportunity is orchestrating handoffs between fragmented tools rather than improving individual engines, but trust requires semantic continuity, formal proof, and auditable evidence with deterministic EDA engines as ground truth. Executives from Siemens EDA, Synopsys, Cadence, Arteris, Axiomise, ChipAgents, Keysight, and Vinci describe token economics, guardrails, and a coming shift from 'productivity' to 'evidence' as the basis of competition.

insights.claim: Siemens EDA's Ankur Gupta says every customer is demanding at least a 2x reduction in time to results, pushing EDA toward faster engines (GPUs, ML, reinforcement learning) without losing confidence in results.
insights.speaker: Ann Steffora Mutschler
insights.so_what: A 2x time-to-results bar sets the benchmark EDA vendors must hit to justify new AI/GPU-accelerated product pricing.
insights.quote: Give me the ability to shrink my time to results by at least 2×
insights.locator: The global shortage of skilled engineers has not gone away

insights.claim: Synopsys' Thomas Andersen says agentic AI only makes sense when token spend is below the cost of the human it replaces and it reduces the cost and complexity of production workflows.
insights.speaker: Ann Steffora Mutschler
insights.so_what: Token cost is now an explicit ROI hurdle for agentic EDA; falling inference prices directly expand the addressable automation market.
insights.quote: If I spend more money on tokens than a human would cost, then it doesn’t make sense
insights.locator: The economics of AI are becoming increasingly important

insights.claim: Letting any agent call any tool is flexible but can be expensive and inefficient if underlying interfaces are poorly written, so EDA vendors aim to pre-integrate so customers avoid unnecessary token and orchestration costs.
insights.speaker: Ann Steffora Mutschler
insights.so_what: Well-engineered agent interfaces become a cost advantage and a lock-in lever for incumbent EDA vendors.
insights.locator: Efficiency also matters at the agent layer

insights.claim: At advanced nodes, design costs can reach hundreds of millions of dollars and a single respin can threaten an entire program, so AI's value depends on accelerating the flow while preserving trust in the results.
insights.speaker: Ann Steffora Mutschler
insights.so_what: High respin costs make customers pay for verification and evidence, supporting verification-focused EDA spending.
insights.locator: AI is arriving in EDA at a time

themes.theme: Handoff loss and the reconciliation tax

insights.claim: Axiomise CEO Ashish Darbari describes chip design as a relay race across dozens of tools from different vendors with different data models and definitions of 'done', where each handoff risks losing information or pushing a locally optimal decision into a globally suboptimal one.
insights.speaker: Ann Steffora Mutschler
insights.so_what: Value is migrating to cross-tool integration layers; vendors with broader flow coverage or neutral data layers gain leverage.
insights.quote: The relay is where most of the pain lives.
insights.locator: Chip design is essentially a relay race

insights.claim: Darbari identifies recurring EDA failure modes: no shared semantic model across vendors, design-to-verification intent loss, closed data formats forcing AI efforts to rebuild parsers, a 'reconciliation tax' of bookkeeping constraints and waivers, and tools hitting local targets while causing downstream closure problems.
insights.speaker: Ann Steffora Mutschler
insights.so_what: These pain points map to product opportunities for interoperability, intent-capture, and cross-boundary optimization startups.
insights.locator: Darbari groups the core workflow challenges

insights.claim: First-time silicon success has fallen sharply, with most respins still traced to design errors, which the article frames as a workflow and intent-transfer problem rather than a compute problem.
insights.speaker: Ann Steffora Mutschler
insights.so_what: Falling first-pass success supports rising verification budgets; throwing more compute at simulation alone will not fix it.
insights.quote: That is a workflow and intent-transfer problem, not simply a compute problem.
insights.locator: Handoff loss between design and verification

insights.claim: A 'Who checks the checkers?' study found that Equifuzz uncovered 16 distinct bugs across three major commercial C-to-RTL equivalence checkers, including unsound cases where non-equivalent designs were declared equivalent.
insights.speaker: Ann Steffora Mutschler
insights.so_what: Even signoff tools are fallible, reinforcing demand for independent verification and evidence trails rather than blind trust in any single vendor's tool.
insights.locator: Trustworthy EDA. Tools also have bugs

insights.claim: Arteris' Andy Nightingale says engineers often act as the integration layer at the system level, and better cross-tool optimization must provide semantic continuity of architectural intent, not merely file-format interoperability.
insights.speaker: Ann Steffora Mutschler
insights.so_what: Arteris positions its system-IP/integration tooling as the carrier of design intent in multi-die flows.
insights.locator: “The same architectural intent may be represented differently

insights.claim: Keysight EDA's Chris Mueth argues AI's biggest near-term EDA impact is in the peripheral process and data-management work around the flow, which holds as much value as core simulators and layout tools, rather than in sign-off.
insights.speaker: Ann Steffora Mutschler
insights.so_what: Workflow/data-management tooling may capture AI value faster than core engines; watch vendors monetizing flow management.
insights.quote: There’s as much value there now as in the core simulators and layout tools
insights.locator: Still, AI’s real impact on EDA will be less about sign-off

insights.claim: ChipAgents' Solaiman Rahim says a DFT-insertion agent coordinating with a timing agent can compress a handoff cycle that takes weeks into potentially hours.
insights.speaker: Ann Steffora Mutschler
insights.so_what: Weeks-to-hours claims on cross-domain handoffs are the productivity metric to watch as agentic EDA startups seek customers.
insights.quote: Instead of taking weeks, it can take potentially just hours.
insights.locator: “If you have a DFT agent handling DFT insertion

insights.claim: Rahim describes an ontology layer that captures why expert engineers avoid certain cells, choose constraints, or debug recurring failures, making that know-how available to less experienced engineers and AI workflows.
insights.speaker: Ann Steffora Mutschler
insights.so_what: Captured tribal knowledge becomes a proprietary data moat for whoever owns the ontology layer.
insights.locator: That speedup requires more than scripts

insights.claim: Darbari says single-tool AI features are becoming table stakes and the next competitive frontier is between tools: agentic orchestration, standardized data models, and moving constraints, waivers, and evidence across boundaries, noting the FluxBench RTL-to-GDSII agent evaluation shows seams remain hard.
insights.speaker: Ann Steffora Mutschler
insights.so_what: Single-tool AI features will not differentiate EDA vendors for long; competition shifts to flow-level orchestration and data standards.
insights.quote: The problem is not the AI. It is the lack of a shared semantic substrate for the AI to reason over.
insights.locator: Further, Darbari observed that single-tool AI features

insights.claim: Darbari outlines three AI layers for reducing cross-tool friction: cross-boundary optimization loops (the most mature use), agentic pipelines and copilots such as Synopsys.ai Copilot, Cadence ChipStack and AuraStack, and Siemens Fuse, and an interoperability layer built on vendor-neutral efforts like Si2's Schema Ontology and Accellera's CDC/RDC Integration Standard.
insights.speaker: Ann Steffora Mutschler
insights.so_what: Maps the competitive products of the big three EDA vendors; vendor-neutral standards could erode lock-in if adopted.
insights.locator: Darbari sees three emerging ways AI can reduce cross-tool friction

insights.claim: Nightingale says AI agents need domain context, consistent representation of intent, controlled permissions, and measurable results, with AI supplying reasoning and orchestration while established EDA engines continue to provide deterministic analysis and verification.
insights.speaker: Ann Steffora Mutschler
insights.so_what: Deterministic incumbent engines stay essential under the agentic layer, protecting core EDA franchises from AI-native disruption.
insights.locator: A fundamental shift in AI’s evolution

insights.claim: Darbari says LLMs can extract properties, suggest assertions, and triage proofs, but generated assertions are hypotheses and only a completed proof against a correct property counts as evidence.
insights.speaker: Ann Steffora Mutschler
insights.so_what: AI raises rather than replaces demand for formal verification engines; bullish for formal tool vendors.
insights.locator: For formal verification, AI is most valuable when handoff loss is high

insights.claim: Cadence's Paul Graykowski describes guardrails where agents propose testbench refactorings or sandboxed regression fixes on a code snapshot and wait for engineer approval rather than changing code unilaterally.
insights.speaker: Ann Steffora Mutschler
insights.so_what: Approval-gated autonomy is the adoption pattern for verification agents; full autonomy is not yet trusted.
insights.locator: These safeguards are being implemented wherever AI is used

insights.claim: Keysight's Mueth says current AI still has room for error, so it should not own specifications or sign-off but should accelerate the workflow around those decisions.
insights.speaker: Ann Steffora Mutschler
insights.so_what: Sign-off remains a human-plus-deterministic-tool domain, preserving incumbent sign-off franchises.
insights.quote: you don’t let it own specifications or sign-off
insights.locator: As part of this, requirements management is essential

insights.claim: Graykowski says checked AI assistance could lower the barrier to formal verification for teams lacking formal expertise by generating candidate properties from intent before code reaches a formal engine such as Jasper.
insights.speaker: Ann Steffora Mutschler
insights.so_what: AI could broaden Cadence Jasper's addressable market beyond formal specialists.
insights.locator: Cadence’s Graykowski noted that kind of checked assistance

insights.claim: Darbari predicts that over the next two to three years AI in EDA will shift from being sold on productivity to being judged on evidence, as safety, security, and automotive customers demand signoff reports stating what is proven, bounded, or unchecked.
insights.speaker: Ann Steffora Mutschler
insights.so_what: Auditability and reproducibility features will become buying criteria, favoring formal and traceability vendors over 'faster convergence' marketing.
insights.quote: The current infatuation with autonomy will give way to an insistence on auditability.
insights.locator: Axiomise’s Darbari pointed to visible shifts

insights.claim: Darbari cites Apple's Hilbert system, which wraps informal LLM reasoning around Lean 4, as the clearest public example of the winning architecture: AI for exploration, formal methods for correctness closure.
insights.speaker: Ann Steffora Mutschler
insights.so_what: Hybrid LLM-plus-formal architectures are the template to track across EDA and other high-assurance software.
insights.quote: AI for exploration. Formal for correctness closure.
insights.locator: The second shift is occurring from simulation confidence to proof-backed signoff

insights.claim: Darbari says AI silicon splits into two verification regimes: training hardware depends on distributed progress, collective operations, and silent-data-corruption resilience, while decode-heavy inference hardware depends on KV-cache ownership, scheduling, isolation, and tail latency, so AI-in-EDA will fragment the same way.
insights.speaker: Ann Steffora Mutschler
insights.so_what: Training and inference chip programs need different verification tooling; specialized vendors may win in each segment.
insights.quote: The cross-tool optimizations that matter for a training accelerator don’t matter for an inference tile.
insights.locator: Another wrinkle is that AI silicon splits

insights.claim: Vinci's Satish Radhakrishnan says much physics-analysis delay happens before the solver starts (geometry cleanup, meshing, materials, handoffs), and an AI front end is useless if simulation still takes hours of setup and days to run.
insights.speaker: Ann Steffora Mutschler
insights.so_what: Agentic value in physics analysis is gated by fast, deterministic solvers; startups solving setup speed have an opening.
insights.quote: Radhakrishnan said much of the delay occurs before a solver starts.
insights.locator: Radhakrishnan said much of the delay occurs before a solver starts

insights.claim: Vinci ingests native design files and pairs pretrained physics models with GPU-native numerical physics kernels to produce solver-accurate results without human meshing or customer-specific training data.
insights.speaker: Ann Steffora Mutschler
insights.so_what: GPU-native physics simulation is an emerging competitive threat to legacy multiphysics solvers.
insights.locator: In Vinci’s case, the approach is to ingest native design files

insights.claim: Connected agent-driven design loops could let engineers evaluate hundreds or thousands of options instead of a handful, turning design exploration from a scheduled event into daily iterative work, while signoff still requires deterministic, reproducible results.
insights.speaker: Ann Steffora Mutschler
insights.so_what: Exploration volume growth implies rising simulation compute consumption, a tailwind for GPU-accelerated EDA.
insights.locator: Radhakrishnan said the first challenge is to remove discrete bottlenecks

insights.claim: ChipAgents' Rahim says semiconductors are becoming a commodity and customers' projects, layouts, and analog experts no longer scale, making customers willing to share layout knowledge for model training.
insights.speaker: Ann Steffora Mutschler
insights.so_what: Customer willingness to share proprietary layout data could give AI-native EDA startups training data previously locked up.
insights.locator: “We are confident we can tackle the problem

insights.claim: Rahim expects workflows to advance over the next six months in root-cause analysis, verification, timing closure, physical design, analog, and advanced packaging, but says complex fully optimized designs remain beyond current frontier models and compute will move up from tools to workflows to chip-design-specific models.
insights.speaker: Ann Steffora Mutschler
insights.so_what: Expect incremental agentic gains in specific workflows, not autonomous end-to-end chip design, in the near term.
insights.locator: Rahim expects workflows to advance over the next six months

insights.claim: Synopsys' Andersen warns that agents built inside individual product groups recreate the silos they are meant to remove, so agentic strategy must be directed top-down across the whole flow.
insights.speaker: Ann Steffora Mutschler
insights.so_what: Organizational execution, not just technology, will separate EDA winners in agentic flows.
insights.locator: Organizational changes required

insights.claim: Movellus CEO Mo Faisal says the earliest agentic AI use is customer ticket triage and support, that teams keep libraries of skill files, and that adoption is advanced in Silicon Valley but not yet happening elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Ann Steffora Mutschler
insights.so_what: Agentic adoption is geographically uneven; early revenue is in support workflows before complex engineering.
insights.locator: Mo Faisal, founder and CEO of Movellus

insights.claim: Cadence's Graykowski frames AI tools as assistants rather than replacements, acting as junior engineers guided by senior human engineers.
insights.speaker: Ann Steffora Mutschler
insights.so_what: Supports augmentation (seat-plus-agent) pricing models rather than headcount replacement narratives.
insights.quote: They’re the junior engineer. You’re the senior engineer.
insights.locator: Graykowski succinctly framed where AI belongs
